name: zscore_reversion_v1
author: claude-4.6-opus
thesis: Pure statistical z-score reversion using a 60-bar lookback (1 hour of 1-min data) identifies when price has deviated >2.0 standard deviations from its rolling 60-bar mean. Unlike VWAP z-score (strategy 2), this uses raw price z-score which captures deviations from the recent trading range rather than volume-weighted fair value. The inefficiency is that short-horizon returns in liquid Indian equities exhibit negative autocorrelation (mean-reverting) at the 1-60 minute horizon. This is empirically documented and arises from market-making dynamics: limit order providers step in after extreme moves, and stop-loss cascades create transient overshoots. The edge persists because the optimal lookback window shifts daily and requires adaptive parameters that most static screeners cannot handle.

long.confirmation: zscore crosses above -1.8 from below -2.0 (initial reversion confirmed)

short.confirmation: zscore crosses below 1.8 from above 2.0 (initial reversion confirmed)

exit.stop_loss: zscore reaches -3.0 (longs) or +3.0 (shorts) — 3-sigma extreme, thesis broken
exit.trailing_stop: trail stop to -1.0 z-score (longs) once z-score crosses -0.5

risk.position_sizing: fixed 1L; volatility-scale using ATR(14)/close to normalize across stocks

filters.vix_filter: India_VIX < 25; in high-vol regimes, z-score extremes are more common but less mean-reverting
filters.time_filter: no entries before 10:00 (need 60 bars of data) or after 14:30
filters.trend_filter: skip if rolling_mean slope > 0.1% per bar (strong intraday trend — z-score will stay extreme)
filters.event_filter: skip on earnings day, RBI policy day
other_filters: Hurst exponent filter: only trade stocks with H < 0.45 on 60-min rolling window

edge.edge_decay_risk: moderate — z-score reversion is well-known but adaptive lookback adds differentiation

weaknesses: 60-bar lookback means signal only available after 10:15 IST — misses the most volatile (and potentially profitable) first hour
Assumes returns are approximately normally distributed; intraday returns have fat tails, making z-score thresholds unreliable
Hurst exponent filter requires significant computation and changes over time — stocks can switch from mean-reverting to trending
prior_art: Z-score mean reversion is foundational in stat arb (Avellaneda & Lee, 2010; Gatev et al., 2006). Applied to single-name intraday rather than pairs. Hurst exponent filtering is discussed in Peters (1994) 'Fractal Market Analysis'. The adaptive lookback approach draws from Kaufman's adaptive moving average concept.
notes: Edge math: 0.57 * 50bps - 0.43 * 40bps = 28.5 - 17.2 = 11.3 bps gross. Costs ~11 bps. Net ≈ 0.3 bps. Essentially breakeven. The Hurst exponent pre-filter is the key differentiator — if it successfully identifies mean-reverting stocks, win rate should be 0.60+, pushing net to ~5 bps. Critical to validate.
